items.title: Why Climate and Energy Entrepreneurs Need Their Own Playbook
items.summary: When Bill Aulet published “Disciplined Entrepreneurship: 24 Steps to a Successful Startup” in 2013, he brought a foundational MIT entrepreneurship framework into the world for any founder to use. But…

guide.notes: When Bill Aulet published “Disciplined Entrepreneurship: 24 Steps to a Successful Startup” in 2013, he brought a foundational MIT entrepreneurship framework into the world for any founder to use. But a climate or energy entrepreneur isn’t just any founder. In teaching MIT’s Climate and Energy Ventures course (formerly Energy Ventures), Aulet, a professor of the practice and the managing director of the Martin Trust Center for MIT Entrepreneurship, and other later instructors of the course found that the standard Disciplined Entrepreneurship framework didn’t fit so snugly in that sector. So they built a new one. Written by MIT entrepreneur in residence Ben Soltoff, with Aulet, Tod Hynes, Francis O’Sullivan, and Libby Wayman, “Disciplined Entrepreneurship for Climate and Energy Ventures,” adapts Aulet’s original framework with climate and energy entrepreneurs in mind. Hear Soltoff explain more about what makes the entrepreneurship journey so different for climate and energy ventures.

items.title: MIT Sloan Professor Emeritus James Utterback 2003 Lecture on Innovation
items.summary: James M. Utterback, PhD '69, Chair, MIT Management of Technology Program; David J. McGrath Professor of Management and Innovation; MIT Sloan School of Management It seems a well-established truth…

guide.notes: James M. Utterback, PhD '69, Chair, MIT Management of Technology Program; David J. McGrath Professor of Management and Innovation; MIT Sloan School of Management It seems a well-established truth that new technologies drive out older, established ones. In this lecture, MIT Sloan Professor James Utterback demonstrates just the opposite, that a symbiotic relationship can evolve between new "predator" and older "prey" industries that can sustain both. Using such vivid historical examples as the lightbulb, safety match and mousetrap, he describes how the original companies that created these products thrived even as they were challenged by newer firms that harnessed automated manufacturing or different distribution methods. Playing a remarkable film shot in 1927, Utterback shows how the transition from ice harvesting to mechanical refrigeration expanded the market for both, exemplifying the idea that new and old business ideas can and often do reinforce each other. About the Speaker: James Utterback was the David J. McGrath jr (1959) Professor of Management and Innovation, Emeritus and…

items.title: The 4CAPS+ Model
items.summary: Great leaders aren’t great at everything — but they don’t have to be. The key is understanding what is "signature" to you and where you want to grow. MIT Sloan professor and @mitleadershipcenter4766…

guide.notes: Great leaders aren’t great at everything — but they don’t have to be. The key is understanding what is "signature" to you and where you want to grow. MIT Sloan professor and @mitleadershipcenter4766 founder Deborah Ancona explains the 4CAPS+ Model, which outlines four key leadership capabilities: sensemaking, relating, visioning, and inventing — with the added “plus” of building credibility. This video breaks down what each of these means, helping you identify your strengths.

items.title: The Next Step: Refining and Expanding Your Signature
items.summary: Understanding your leadership signature is just the beginning. Once you’ve built a strong foundation, the next step is to refine and expand it. By exploring different leadership frameworks — like the…

guide.notes: Understanding your leadership signature is just the beginning. Once you’ve built a strong foundation, the next step is to refine and expand it. By exploring different leadership frameworks — like the 4CAPS+ model — you can add new dimensions that enhance your unique approach. MIT Sloan professor and @mitleadershipcenter4766 founder Deborah Ancona encourages us to ask: What truly resonates with me? What strengths can I build on? Leadership is not static; it evolves as you grow and adapt.

items.title: Highlighting Different Aspects of Your Leadership Signature
items.summary: Your leadership signature isn’t static — it shifts with your role, your team, and your goals. Right now, what aspect of your leadership do you want to highlight? Maybe it’s your ability to navigate…

guide.notes: Your leadership signature isn’t static — it shifts with your role, your team, and your goals. Right now, what aspect of your leadership do you want to highlight? Maybe it’s your ability to navigate change, foster collaboration, or drive results. Whatever it is, the best way to showcase it is through the stories you tell. MIT Sloan Professor Deborah Ancona asks us to take a moment to reflect: What’s most important to communicate at this stage in your career? And what real examples bring that to life?

items.title: Telling Your Leadership Story
items.summary: Your leadership signature isn’t just what you say — it’s what you do and how others experience it. MIT Sloan professor and @mitleadershipcenter4766 founder Deborah Ancona explains that the most…

guide.notes: Your leadership signature isn’t just what you say — it’s what you do and how others experience it. MIT Sloan professor and @mitleadershipcenter4766 founder Deborah Ancona explains that the most effective leaders don’t just describe their leadership style in broad terms; they bring it to life through real stories and actions. Instead of saying, “I’m collaborative” or “I empower my team,” think about a moment when your leadership made an impact. Did you adjust a project based on your team’s input? Did you create space for new ideas that changed the course of a decision? By thinking of these stories, you make your leadership signature clear and inspire others to do the same.

items.title: What Images Best Represent You as a Leader?
items.summary: Leadership isn’t one-size-fits-all, and traditional categories — autocratic, empathetic, servant leader — might not fully capture your unique style. So instead of words, let’s start with pictures.…

guide.notes: Leadership isn’t one-size-fits-all, and traditional categories — autocratic, empathetic, servant leader — might not fully capture your unique style. So instead of words, let’s start with pictures. You might find that multiple images reflect different facets of your leadership — perhaps you’re both an innovator and an empath, a strategist and a coach. Once you’ve chosen your images, put your leadership signature into words.

guide.notes: Yesterday I posted a video explaining why Dave Ramsey’s claim that retirees can safely spend 8% of their portfolios did not make sense. I realized after posting that his claim was even worse than I initially thought. The S&P 500 returned around 12% per year 1926-2022 measured as an arithmetic average. Measured as a geometric average, which is what matters to investors, it has been closer to 10%.
